items.prompt: What changes when a person's influence reaches organizational scale?
choices: Which skills they have to master
The number of people a misuse reaches
What honesty demands of them in each room
items.explanation: The skills stay the same. What grows is the number of people downstream of each choice.

items.prompt: Who mostly pays when someone's reach is narrow?
choices: Mostly the person who made the misstep
Mostly the whole organization
Mostly the colleagues sitting closest to them
items.explanation: A narrow-reach misstep stalls a review or bruises a relationship, and that is mostly the person's own cost.

items.prompt: What does 'influence at scale' mean here?
choices: They hold a high-ranking title
Most colleagues like them
Their framing or objection reliably changes what the whole org decides
items.explanation: It is about reliably changing org-level decisions, not about title or popularity.

items.prompt: How does drift at org scale relate to the earlier idea of identity drift?
choices: Same mechanism, with the bill sent to more people
A separate mechanism that only appears at scale
The mechanism fades once more people are watching
items.explanation: Drift is still a chain of individually defensible compromises. Only the number of people who pay for it grows.

items.prompt: Why can people affected by a wide-reach decision rarely correct it?
choices: They are always too busy to push back
They have been told not to disagree
They never see the choice being made
items.explanation: Downstream people are outside the room, so a peer's chance to push back does not exist for them.

items.prompt: Does this unit add a new political skill?
choices: No, it asks what existing skills serve
Yes, a skill for reading hidden agendas
Yes, a way to avoid conflict
items.explanation: The skills were built earlier. This unit is about the target they serve once enough people depend on them.

items.prompt: In the L1 teaching model, how does the people-affected count grow with reach?
choices: In a perfectly straight line
Faster than steadily, bending upward as reach grows
It levels off after a point
items.explanation: The model uses scale to the power 2.1, so each extra step of reach adds more people than the last.

items.prompt: In that model, roughly how many people does scale 8 affect?
choices: About 8
About 79
About 800
items.explanation: 8 to the power 2.1 is about 79. It is an assumed teaching model, not measured data.

items.prompt: Two engineers handle a disagreement the same bad way. One works on a single team's tooling. The other's objection reliably decides company-wide launches. What differs?
choices: Same drift mechanism, but the second one's cost lands on many people who never saw the choice
Different mechanisms, because the second one needs a separate skill set to avoid the same kind of mistake
Same mechanism, but the first one's mistake is worse because that person has less standing to absorb it
No difference, because both mistakes can be repaired afterward by raising the matter in another meeting
items.explanation: The skills and the mechanism are identical. Only the number of unseen people who pay changes.
items.reference:
Same skills, bigger bill
narrow reach: mostly I pay
org-wide reach: people who never saw the choice pay
mechanism of drift: unchanged
Why: reach does not change the skills or the drift mechanism, it changes how many people the cost lands on.
items.learnMore:
Why the stakes rise with reach

The skills in this track do not change shape as influence widens. What changes is who sits downstream: people who were not in the room and cannot correct a bad call the way a peer could.

Common mistake

Assuming the earlier units already settle the question. They were built around costs that mostly land on the person choosing.
items.reflection: Think of someone whose word moves decisions far beyond their own team. Who is downstream of their choices that never hears them being made?

items.prompt: A reviewer says the earlier units already cover wide-reach influence, so this unit is redundant. What is the gap in that reasoning?
choices: Those units skipped drift entirely, so this unit introduces the mechanism for the first time ever
Those units taught the wrong skills, so the skills must be rebuilt from scratch at this level
Those units assumed costs mostly land on the chooser, and wide reach moves them onto others
Nothing, since those units covered everything and this one only repeats them for revision
items.explanation: The skills are the same but the stakes are not, so the question of what they serve needs its own test.

items.prompt: Someone with wide reach softens a concern here and delays a disclosure there, each time defensibly. Why is that harder to catch than the same pattern with narrow reach?
choices: Wide-reach people are far better at hiding what they are really doing from observers
Narrow-reach roles never involve defensible compromises that could add up over time
Larger organizations have no norms of any kind that could flag the pattern to anyone

items.explanation: Drift stays invisible when the cost lands on people who never see the choice and cannot object.

items.prompt: What is the first of the two questions?
choices: Does this make the decision more likely to be right, or only to go my way?
Will this move succeed?
Will my manager approve?
items.explanation: The first question separates improving the decision from steering the outcome.

items.prompt: What is the second of the two questions?
choices: Would colleagues applaud this once it was over?
Would my real reasoning hold up if everyone saw it?
Could I get away with it without anyone noticing at all?
items.explanation: The visibility test is about exposing the real reasoning, not about earning praise.

items.prompt: Why is 'will it work' a poor test?
choices: It is too hard to measure in advance
Good and bad motives both succeed
It only applies to technical decisions
items.explanation: Both a sincere concern and a self-serving one can succeed, so success tells you nothing about which it was.

items.prompt: What is 'outcome control'?
choices: Making sure the final decision turns out correct
Steering a result to a chosen answer, even the safest for me
Deciding which people are invited to a meeting about it and when
items.explanation: Outcome control is aimed at the answer you want, regardless of whether it is right.

items.prompt: Staying quiet about a risk because the project's champion is useful. What is the verdict?
choices: Passes both questions
Passes only the first
Fails both questions
items.explanation: Silence withholds information that could change the decision, and the honest reason would not survive being said aloud.

items.prompt: Does the visibility test ask whether the move would be praised?
choices: Yes, praise is the whole point of the test
No, only whether the real reasoning is fully visible
Yes, but only praise from your own manager
items.explanation: A well-meant wrong call is uncomfortable but passes. The test targets self-protective reasoning.

items.prompt: A real risk is timed to land just before your own promotion review. What is the verdict?
choices: Both pass, since the risk is real
Both fail, since any risk talk at review time is self-serving
Content passes, execution fails
items.explanation: The risk is real, but the timing serves the mover and would not survive full visibility.

items.prompt: Talking to the people a proposal affects before proposing it. What is the verdict?
choices: Legitimate: it holds up in the open
Self-serving lobbying
Neutral, no effect on the verdict
items.explanation: Checking with affected people surfaces concerns early and nobody is ambushed.

items.prompt: An engineer raises a well-founded concern about a colleague's design in a large cross-team meeting, not in the design review where the decision is made. What does the test say?
choices: Everything passes, because the concern is true and truth is the only criterion that matters here
Everything fails, because raising any concern about a colleague's work is a self-serving act
The content passes, but the venue fails because it serves visible standing over the decision
Nothing can be said, because the choice of venue is a matter of taste outside the test
items.explanation: Truth of the content does not legitimize a venue picked to maximize someone's embarrassment.
items.reference:
The two questions
1. does it make the decision more likely RIGHT, or just go my way?
2. would the real reasoning survive being seen by everyone affected?
content can pass while venue or timing fails
Why: 'will it work' cannot separate a good-faith concern from a self-serving one, but these two questions can.
items.learnMore:
Judging the execution, not only the content

A concern can be completely legitimate and still be deployed in a way that serves the mover. Venue, timing, and framing each get checked against the same two questions.

Common mistake

Treating 'the concern is true' as the end of the analysis. Truth of the content does not legitimize every way of using it.
items.reflection: Recall a time you raised a concern or pushed an idea. Would your real reasons for the venue and timing have held up if everyone could see them?

items.prompt: Someone stays silent on a risk, partly from genuine doubt and partly because the director is useful. Which question exposes the self-interested part?
choices: The visibility question, since 'I did not want to spend capital' would fail when said aloud
The success question, since silence could clearly never work out as a strategy in the end
Neither question, since mixed motives cannot be separated by either of them in practice
The first question alone, since doubt and usefulness are exactly the same thing underneath it all
items.explanation: Genuine doubt survives being said aloud. The wish to keep a useful relationship does not.

Persuasiveness is random, so no principle could ever distinguish between the two
Both kinds of move can succeed, so the difference lies in the reasoning behind each
items.explanation: Success is available to both, which is why the test examines purpose and visibility instead.

It fails, because visibility alone can never be enough to justify a decision that went wrong
It cannot be applied, because the test only works on decisions that turn out to be good ones
items.explanation: Wrong but honest reasoning is a different failure from self-protective reasoning.

items.prompt: What is 'entangled self-interest'?
choices: Legitimate influence and personal benefit cannot be fully separated
A conflict of interest to report
A habit of always putting yourself first
items.explanation: Doing the job well also builds your reputation, so the two overlap by nature.

items.prompt: Is a reputation for good judgment a corruption of the job?
choices: Yes, it always taints judgment afterward
Yes, once colleagues start to notice it
No, it comes with doing the job well
items.explanation: Being seen as effective is a normal result of doing the work well.

items.prompt: How often do the org's good and my interest point the same way?
choices: Almost never
Most of the time
About half the time
items.explanation: Most good uses of influence serve both at once, which is a healthy incentive structure.

items.prompt: Where does the discipline actually apply?
choices: At every decision, to the same degree
At the rare moments the two diverge
Only when watched
items.explanation: Divergence is rare, which is why it is easy to miss or rationalize.

items.prompt: At the fork, what is the real test?
choices: Whether you had a stake at all
Whether anyone complains afterward
Which branch you choose
items.explanation: Having a stake is normal. Choosing the stake over the org's good at the fork is the failure.

items.prompt: Why is claiming 'I have no stake' unhelpful?
choices: It sounds unfriendly to peers
Others always catch the lie
It hides the fork from you, so you cannot notice it
items.explanation: If you cannot see the overlap, you will not notice when it splits.

items.prompt: Is having a stake in the outcome disqualifying?
choices: No, it is the normal condition of the job
Yes, always
Yes, unless you tell your manager and the whole team
items.explanation: The stake is expected. The question is what you do when it points away from the org's good.

items.prompt: Which is the actual failure this unit names?
choices: Ever benefiting from good work
Building a reputation among colleagues over many years
Choosing your safety over the org's good at the fork
items.explanation: Benefit from good work is fine. Picking the self-protective branch at the divergence is the failure.

items.prompt: A colleague says, 'I have no stake in this launch, so my judgment is clean.' Why is 'I have a stake, and here is the moment I will watch' more reliable?
choices: Claiming no stake is always a deliberate lie that other colleagues will quickly detect in practice
Naming the stake and the moment gives you something concrete to check when the fork arrives
Having a stake guarantees correct judgment, so naming it is the same as proving it is sound
Stakes only matter once they are written down, so the writing is the real safeguard here
items.explanation: A denied overlap is invisible to you, and an invisible fork cannot be noticed.
items.reference:
Overlap and the fork
most of the time: org's good and my interest align (fine)
rarely: they diverge (the fork)
at the fork: which branch do I choose?
Why: having a stake is the normal condition of the role, so the discipline is noticing and choosing at the fork, not removing the stake.
items.learnMore:
Why self-interest cannot be removed

A reputation for good judgment is both what doing the job well produces and what protects a career. Denying that makes the overlap invisible to you, which is how a fork gets missed.

Common mistake

Believing a clean conscience means having no stake. The honest position names the stake and the moment to watch for.
items.reflection: Think of a decision where doing right and protecting yourself pointed different ways. Did you notice the fork while it was happening?

items.prompt: Raising a real risk both helps the launch and boosts the person's standing. What should they do?

Delay until the benefit disappears, so the motive can later be verified as entirely pure
Hand the concern to someone else, because the benefit makes the original person biased
Proceed, since alignment is the normal case and is not a warning sign by itself
items.explanation: Overlap is the common case. Divergence is what needs watching.

items.prompt: Into how many parts does Marcus separate his hesitation?
choices: One: plain fear of the director
Three: fear, anger, and pride among others
Two: real uncertainty and self-protection
items.explanation: He names genuine technical uncertainty and a self-protective wish not to pay a cost.

items.prompt: What should genuine uncertainty affect?
choices: How he states the concern
Whether he raises it at all
Who he invites to the meeting
items.explanation: Uncertainty means framing it as something to check, not dropping it.

items.prompt: Where does Marcus raise the concern?
choices: In a private email to Priya alone
In the launch review that sets the date
At the next steering review, two weeks out
items.explanation: He picks the room where the decision is actually finalized.

items.prompt: When does he raise it relative to the date?
choices: After it ships
Two weeks earlier
Three days out, while it can still change the outcome
items.explanation: Timing it for information, while the decision can still change, keeps it clean.

items.prompt: How does he frame the concern?
choices: An accusation that the team was careless
A factual sequence, with his uncertainty stated
A confident certainty meant to force the delay on the team
items.explanation: A specific sequence with a stated limit holds up said aloud.

items.prompt: What does doing right cost Marcus?
choices: A formal reprimand from leadership
A lasting chill with Priya
Nothing, since he was right
items.explanation: The story deliberately keeps a real, quiet cost.

items.prompt: Why does the story avoid a cost-free ending?
choices: It would imply doing this right is always safe
Costs make the story longer
Real stories never end well
items.explanation: The test was never a promise that the right choice is also the safe one.

items.prompt: If the check had found nothing, was raising it still justified?
choices: No, a false alarm is always a failure
Only if Priya agrees it was reasonable afterward
Yes, it made the decision better informed
items.explanation: The first question asks whether raising improves the decision, which it does either way.

items.prompt: Marcus considers staying quiet because he has not reproduced the bug. What is the flaw in that reason?
choices: It is sound, since a concern that cannot be reproduced should never be raised at all
It overlooks that only a director may decide whether an uncertain risk is worth raising
It is sound, because certainty is the minimum a concern needs before it is spoken
It treats uncertainty as a reason to withhold, when it only justifies careful framing
items.explanation: Uncertainty shapes the framing. Raising it lets people with more context check.
items.reference:
Marcus's move, checked
content: a checkable sequence, uncertainty stated
venue: the review where the date is set
timing: 3 days out, still changeable (story assumption)
cost: a lasting chill with Priya
Why: uncertainty changes how you state a concern, not whether you raise it, and a correct move can still carry a real cost.
items.learnMore:
Execution and honest cost

Sorting a hesitation into genuine uncertainty and self-protection lets the first shape how you phrase a concern while denying the second a vote on whether to raise it.

Common mistake

Using real uncertainty as cover for silence. It lets a legitimate caution do the work of a self-protective motive.
items.reflection: Think of a time you hesitated to speak up. How much of the hesitation was real uncertainty, and how much was protecting yourself?
